stops.name: Georgia State Capitol
stops.description: The dome above you is sheathed in gold leaf hauled down from Dahlonega, the town where Georgia's 1830s gold rush happened, which is why the legislature is said to meet under the Gold Dome.

stops.name: Atlanta City Hall
stops.description: This 1930 Gothic Revival tower stands on the ground where General Sherman set up his headquarters during the 1864 occupation of Atlanta.

stops.name: Shrine of the Immaculate Conception
stops.address: 48 Martin Luther King Jr Dr SW
stops.description: Atlanta's oldest church survived the burning of the city because its pastor, Father Thomas O'Reilly, talked a Union general out of torching it.

stops.name: Statue of Henry W. Grady
stops.description: Unveiled in 1891 before a crowd of about 25,000 at the corner of Marietta and Forsyth, this bronze honors the newspaper editor who sold the country on the phrase New South.

stops.name: Healey Building
stops.description: Look for the missing half: this Gothic Revival tower was meant to be one of two joined by a block-long atrium, but World War I and its owner's death in 1920 killed the twin.

stops.name: Flatiron Building
stops.description: Atlanta's oldest standing skyscraper wedged into its triangular lot in 1897, five years before New York built the Flatiron everybody has heard of.

stops.name: Woodruff Park
stops.description: The bronze woman releasing a bird here is Atlanta from the Ashes, the city's phoenix, and the park itself was bought anonymously by Coca-Cola's Robert Woodruff, whose name went on it only after he was found out.

stops.name: Hurt Building
stops.description: An 18-story wedge from 1913 with a three-story domed rotunda inside, it was the first home of the Federal Reserve Bank of Atlanta.

stops.name: Candler Building
stops.description: Coca-Cola magnate Asa Candler put up the city's tallest building in 1906 and covered it in carved marble; it is a hotel now, with the lobby left intact.

stops.name: APEX Museum
stops.description: Atlanta's Black history museum has held the same 1910 John Wesley Dobbs building since 1978, back when it was still a tire warehouse.

stops.name: Big Bethel AME Church
stops.description: Sweet Auburn's oldest congregation ran the city's first public school for Black children out of its basement and hosted Morris Brown College's first classes in 1881.

stops.name: Odd Fellows Building and Auditorium
stops.description: Booker T. Washington dedicated this red brick lodge in 1912, and its auditorium next door was the only major hall in Atlanta where Black audiences could sit on the main floor.

stops.name: Prince Hall Masonic Temple
stops.description: The Southern Christian Leadership Conference opened its first office in this yellow brick lodge in 1957, and Martin Luther King Jr. worked for years from a windowless room inside it.

stops.name: Ebenezer Baptist Church Heritage Sanctuary
stops.description: Martin Luther King Jr. was baptized here, served as co-pastor beside his father from 1960 until his death, and was mourned here at his funeral in April 1968.

stops.name: Martin Luther King Jr. Birth Home
stops.description: King was born in an upstairs bedroom of this 1895 Queen Anne house in 1929 and lived here until he was twelve; park rangers still run free tours inside.

note: Atlanta has never come up in this file's history, so it won outright over the other cities that have not run. The batch is one walk: the government cluster at the south end (Capitol, City Hall, the Shrine), north through Five Points and Fairlie-Poplar (Grady, Healey, Flatiron, Woodruff Park, Hurt, Candler), then east along Auburn Avenue through Sweet Auburn to the King birth home. Ends to end is roughly a mile and a half, longer than a tight loop but it is exactly how Atlanta's historic core reads on foot. Every ZIP was looked up against the verified street address; the only null is the Grady statue, which sits in a traffic island at Marietta and Forsyth with no street number of its own. Dropped: the Atlanta Zero Mile Post, because the real marker was moved to the Atlanta History Center in Buckhead in 2018 and only a replica stands downtown; Underground Atlanta, whose lower level closed in 2017 and whose redevelopment status is unsettled; the Auburn Avenue Research Library and Central Presbyterian Church, both verified and both fine stops, held back only to keep the batch at fifteen; and the Atlanta Constitution Building at 143 Alabama St SW, which still stands and is worth a look but has been vacant since 1972 and is now a fenced redevelopment site. The article-level sweep found dozens more downtown towers (Equitable, William-Oliver, Rhodes-Haverty and the like) that would pad the list without adding much for a visitor on foot.
